key_insight: Workload flexibility in behind-the-meter data centers only becomes useful when scheduling is co-optimized with converter and network limits, so computing demand can be shifted without violating electrical constraints.
engineering_relevance: The paper shows how to turn data-center computing flexibility into physically realizable power flexibility by coordinating workloads with photovoltaic generation, storage, and grid purchases.
method: Task-level MILP preserves training synchronicity and completion constraints.
Inference pooling is convexified with Minkowski-sum aggregation and Shapley–Folkman relaxation to avoid unit-level binaries.
A four-node electrical model with lifted voltages and SOCP links computing demand to converter, voltage, and grid limits.
evidence_signal: Case studies indicate that electrical constraints materially reshape scheduling and renewable use, and coordinated scheduling achieves negligible inference shortage while matching the original AC model in verification.
watch_item: The approach depends on accurate electrical-modeling and converter-limit data; if these are mismodeled, schedules may still trigger overloads or voltage violations in practice.
paper_title: Converter-Aware Coordination of Computing Flexibility in Behind-the-Meter Data Centers
